entries.narration: Let's start with the idea everything else in this course rests on. There are broadly three ways to change infrastructure. The oldest is an imperative script: create the network, create the first server, create the second. It runs steps in order, and if you run it a second time, it happily does the work again, and now you have four servers. Configuration management tools like Ansible, Chef and Puppet solve a different problem: they shape what runs inside a server that already exists, the packages, files and services. Terraform takes the third approach. You declare the objects you want to exist, the network and the two servers, and Terraform compares that declaration with what it has recorded, then proposes only the actions needed to close the gap. Run it a second time and it says no changes, because there is no gap left. That convergence is what gives you a plan you can read before anything happens, and environments you can rebuild from reviewed files. But keep one limit in mind from the very start. Terraform can tell you the objects exist as declared. It cannot tell you your application works. That needs its own checks.

When you run Terraform, two kinds of program are involved, and knowing which one does what will save you a lot of confusion later. The first is Terraform core, the CLI binary itself. Core reads your configuration and your state, works out how resources depend on each other, builds a graph from that, computes the plan, and records the results in state. What core does not do is talk to any cloud. That is the job of providers. A provider is a plugin that knows one platform: its resource types, the schema of arguments and attributes each type has, and how to turn create, update and delete into calls against that platform's API. Core talks to providers, and providers talk to the APIs. This chapter's example uses terraform data, which is built into Terraform itself. There is nothing to download, no API, and no credentials, which makes it a safe place to learn the workflow. A real cloud resource, like an S3 bucket, is different: init has to download the AWS provider, the provider needs credentials from your environment, and the API on the other end has the final say on what actually exists.

Here is the distinction that makes plans readable. When people say the infrastructure, they can mean four different things. First, the configuration: the files you write, describing what you want. Second, the state: Terraform's record, after an apply, that the address terraform data dot release is bound to one particular object, with that object's ID and the attributes it had at the time. Third, the observed attributes: what the provider reads back from the API when Terraform refreshes. And fourth, the real object itself, which exists outside Terraform and can be changed by a person in a console or by another tool. A plan is Terraform comparing these layers: configuration against the state, after refreshing the state against what the provider observes. Two consequences follow straight away. State is a record, not the truth, so reality can drift away from it, and we will deal with drift properly in chapter four. And state stores every attribute in plain JSON, including passwords and keys when a resource has them. So treat the state file as sensitive from your very first apply. Don't commit it, and don't paste it into a ticket.

Terraform configuration is written in a language called HCL, and the whole of our first file uses just four pieces of grammar. The first is the block. A block has a type, then some labels, then a body in braces. Resource, terraform data, release is a block of type resource with two labels: the resource type and a name you choose. The second is the argument: a name, an equals sign and a value inside a body, like default equals one point oh point oh. The third is the reference. An expression like var dot app version doesn't contain a value itself. It reads one from somewhere else, here from the variable block. References also tell Terraform which things depend on which, which matters a great deal in chapter three. The fourth is the address. Resource type dot name, terraform data dot release, names exactly one resource, and it is the name you will see in plans, in state and in commands. With those four, the file reads cleanly: a terraform block pinning the version of the CLI, a variable taking input, a resource declaring an object, and an output exposing a value once it exists.

Now let's run it, in six steps. terraform init prepares the working directory. It installs the providers the configuration needs, and for a real provider it writes a lock file recording exactly which version was chosen. terraform fmt rewrites your files into the one canonical style, so that reviews are about meaning rather than spacing. terraform validate checks syntax, references and types without calling any API, so it can catch a misspelled variable before anything is touched. Then terraform plan, with dash out, proposes the changes and saves them to a file. The output on the left is a real run. The plus sign means create: the address terraform data dot release has no object bound to it yet, so Terraform will make one. Some attributes say known after apply, because their values only exist once the object has been created. And the summary line, one to add, zero to change, zero to destroy, is the first thing to read in every plan. terraform show, given that file, prints the saved plan again so it can be reviewed. Finally, terraform apply with that saved file carries out exactly the actions you reviewed and nothing else. One caution: a saved plan can contain sensitive values, so protect it as carefully as state.

Once apply has finished, terraform output prints the values the configuration chose to expose. Here that is the release object, with app shop and version one point oh point oh. Now the lifecycle continues. Change the app version to one point one point oh and plan again. This time the symbol is a tilde, which means update in-place: the same object, with the same ID, gets changed rather than replaced. Notice that the plan only shows what differs and hides the unchanged attribute. Later in the course you will meet the more dangerous symbol, minus slash plus, which means replace: by default, destroy the old object and then create a new one with a new ID. Destruction itself is something you do deliberately. terraform plan dash destroy previews it, terraform destroy carries it out, and the plan shows minus signs with every value going to null. For terraform data that is harmless. For a database it means the data is gone, not paused, and no Terraform command brings it back. And remember the limit from the start of the chapter: neither of these plans can tell you whether your application still works afterwards. Successful apply means the API accepted the change. Nothing more.

In chapter one everything lived in a single file. Real configurations are split across several, so let's be precise about what Terraform actually reads. The directory you run Terraform in is called the root module, and Terraform loads every file ending in dot t f, or dot t f dot json, in that directory, and nothing from its subfolders. All of those files become one configuration with one namespace. That is why declaring a variable called region in two different files is an error, as you can see on the left: Terraform does not care which file a block lives in. The file names you see here, versions, providers, variables, locals, main and outputs, are a convention for the people reading the code, not something Terraform enforces. And here is the point that trips people up: file order is not execution order. Terraform works out what to do first from references between blocks, not from the order of files or lines. Beside the configuration sit a few other things: a tfvars file that supplies values, the lock file that records provider versions, and the dot terraform folder of downloaded plugins, which never belongs in version control.

A configuration is written against particular versions of Terraform and of its providers, and it should say so. Without version requirements, a fresh init simply installs the newest releases, which is how a configuration that worked last month stops working today. Both requirements live in the terraform block, usually in a file called versions dot t f. required version constrains the Terraform CLI itself. If someone runs the configuration with a version outside the range, Terraform stops before doing anything, which is the error you can see at the bottom left. required providers lists each provider the configuration uses, with its source address and a version range. The source hashicorp slash aws is short for registry dot terraform dot io slash hashicorp slash aws, and the key aws is the local name this configuration uses for it. Now the operators. Equals pins one exact version. Greater-than-or-equal accepts anything newer, including the next major version, which is usually too loose. The pessimistic operator, tilde greater-than, is the common choice. Tilde greater-than six point zero accepts any six point x release and never seven, because major versions are where breaking changes go.

A version range says what is allowed. The lock file records what was actually chosen. When terraform init selects a provider version, it writes it to dot terraform dot lock dot h c l, together with the constraints it satisfied and checksums of the package it installed. Commit this file. With it in version control, everyone on the team, and every pipeline, installs exactly the same provider versions, and if a downloaded package does not match a recorded checksum, init refuses to continue. The lock also changes how upgrades happen. On the left, the constraint was widened to allow any three point x release. A plain init kept the locked version, three point eight point one, because it still satisfies the constraint. Only init dash upgrade went looking for the newest allowed version and moved the lock to three point nine point one. That makes an upgrade a deliberate, reviewable change: the lock file diff shows up in your pull request, and you plan before you apply. Two things the lock does not cover. It does not lock module versions, so pin those in each module block. And it only holds checksums for the platforms it has seen, which terraform providers lock can extend.

Declaring a provider and configuring it are two different things. required providers says which provider the configuration needs. A provider block says how to use it: which region, which account, which endpoint. On the left, the first aws block has no alias, so it is the default configuration, using the region from a variable. The second block adds alias equals d r and a different region. That is a second, independent configuration of the same provider plugin. Resources use the default unless they opt in, and the replica bucket does exactly that with provider equals aws dot d r. The plan for this configuration places one bucket in each region. Recent versions of the AWS provider also accept a region argument on individual resources, but aliases remain the general mechanism, because they can also carry different accounts and different credentials. Which brings us to credentials. They do not belong in configuration. Supply them from the environment, through a profile, single sign-on, or the identity of your CI system, because anything written into a dot t f file ends up in Git history. The error at the bottom is what happens with none available: each provider configuration fails separately, here the d r alias.

Variables are how a configuration takes input, and in Terraform every variable can, and usually should, have a type. On the left, the environment variable is an object with four named attributes: a name, an instance count, and two optional attributes with defaults, size and tags. Types do real work. Every value is checked against the type before planning starts, so passing the word two as an instance count fails immediately with a clear error, instead of producing something strange halfway through an apply. Optional attributes are filled in when they are left out, or set to null, which is why the console shows size as small even though the tfvars file never mentioned it. This variable has no default, which makes it required: a value must arrive from somewhere. And there are several somewheres. In increasing order of precedence: the default, environment variables starting with T F underscore VAR, the terraform dot tfvars file, any dot auto dot tfvars files in alphabetical order, and finally dash var and dash var-file on the command line. A later source replaces the whole value. If two files both set environment, the objects are not merged; the later one wins outright.

Two more kinds of named value. A local value gives a name to something derived from other values, so it is computed once and reused. Here, name prefix combines the word shop with the environment name, and web names builds one name per instance from it. Locals are internal: nothing outside the configuration can set them, which is exactly what separates them from variables. An output goes the other way. It exposes a value to whoever runs this configuration, printed after apply and readable later with terraform output. In chapter five, when we build modules, outputs become even more important, because they are the only thing a calling configuration can see of a module. So give them descriptions and treat them as a contract. Now look at the password. Because db password comes from a variable marked sensitive, Terraform refuses to output it unless the output is marked sensitive as well, to confirm you meant it. And on the left, terraform output shows it redacted. But redacted is not hidden. terraform output dash json prints the real value, and the state file holds it in plain text. Sensitive controls display, not storage, and we come back to that properly in chapter eight.

Anywhere Terraform expects a value, you can write an expression instead, and the quickest way to learn them is terraform console. Run it in a configuration's directory and you can evaluate expressions against that configuration's variables and locals, which is exactly what the left side shows. Expressions are built from a few families. Operators do arithmetic, comparison and logic, so two times the instance count plus one is five, and the comparison returns true. Functions transform values. Terraform ships a large library of them, upper, join, cidrsubnet for carving networks into subnets, and many more, but you cannot write your own functions in the language itself. Collections are indexed with square brackets, and lookup reads a map key with a fallback when it is missing. Then there are types, and Terraform converts between them automatically when it safely can. The string five plus one is six. A set removes duplicates and keeps no order of its own. But conversion has limits: tonumber of the word two is an error. The console is read-only. It never changes infrastructure, so it is a safe place to check an expression before it goes into a plan.

The next group of constructs generates values from other values. A conditional, condition question mark a colon b, picks one of two values, so the same configuration can run three servers in production and one everywhere else. A for expression transforms a collection. In square brackets it builds a list, here upper-casing every web name. In braces it builds a map, with an arrow between key and value. Add an if clause and it filters. And templates can loop too, with percent-brace for directives inside a string. Then there is one construct that generates something other than a value. Some resource arguments are nested blocks, like the ingress rules of a security group, and you cannot build a block with an expression. A dynamic block can. For each element of var dot web ports, it writes one ingress block, and inside content, ingress dot key and ingress dot value refer to the current element. The plan at the bottom shows the result: two ingress blocks, http and https, generated from a two-entry map. Two limits. Dynamic only produces nested blocks inside a resource, never whole resources; that is for each, in chapter three. And used too freely, it hides what the configuration actually says.

Not everything a configuration needs is something it should manage. A shared network built by another team, a machine image published by your platform group, the account you happen to be running in: you need to use them, but they are not yours to create or destroy. That is what data sources are for. A data block reads an existing object and makes its attributes available, and its address always starts with data dot. On the left, data dot local file dot release notes reads a file that someone else maintains, and the resource uses its contents. Look at the plan: the read happens first, during planning, and the value it found flows straight into the planned input. Compare the two kinds of block. Terraform creates, updates and destroys a resource. It only ever reads a data source. That makes a data source an external dependency. If the object changes, your next plan changes with it. If it disappears, the plan fails. So read what you depend on, and manage only what you own. One more detail: when a data source depends on a value that is not known until apply, Terraform waits and reads it during apply instead, and the plan shows that.

In chapter two we said file order is not execution order. Here is what Terraform uses instead. Every time one block refers to another, that reference becomes an edge in a dependency graph. The web config file reads the network's generated ID, so web depends on network. The database file does the same. The monitoring file refers to both of their filenames, so it depends on both. You never declared any of these dependencies. They are implicit, and they come straight from the references you had to write anyway. terraform graph prints the graph it built, and the diagram on the left is that output. Then Terraform walks the graph. Look at the real apply log underneath. Network is created first. Then web and db start together, because there is no edge between them, so nothing forces an order. Only when both have finished does monitoring start. By default Terraform runs up to ten operations at the same time, and the dash parallelism flag changes that. And when you destroy, the graph is walked in reverse: monitoring goes first, because something that depends on an object must be removed before the object it depends on.

The graph only contains the dependencies Terraform can see, and it can only see references. Look at this configuration. A resource writes a config file, and a data source reads the same file. But the data source names the file by its path, written out as a plain string. There is no reference to the resource, so as far as Terraform knows, the two are unrelated. Data sources are normally read during planning, so the read happens immediately, before the file has been created, and the plan fails, exactly as you see on the left. There are two fixes. The best one is to make the relationship a reference: set the filename to local file dot web dot filename. Now the dependency is part of the graph, and Terraform defers the read until apply. When there is genuinely nothing to reference, the explicit fallback is depends on, which adds the edge by hand. But depends on has a cost. The data source is now read during apply, so everything derived from it is unknown in the plan, and a broad depends on can make whole sections of a plan vaguer than they need to be. And at the bottom, the opposite problem: two blocks that refer to each other form a cycle, and Terraform cannot order them at all.

Plans are made before anything is created, so some values simply do not exist yet. A generated name, a cloud-assigned ID, an IP address: the plan shows these as known after apply. That is normal, and Terraform handles it well. On the left, the tag resource takes the generated pet name as its input, and it plans without complaint. Its own output becomes unknown too, and everything is filled in during apply. Keys are a different matter. for each and count decide how many instances of a resource exist, and what each one is called. A plan has to answer that question, because the number of instances is the plan. So when the web resource tries to build its for each keys from the generated name, Terraform stops with the error you can see: the keys depend on something that cannot be determined until apply. The fix is a design rule worth remembering. Keep keys static, written in your configuration, and let only the values attached to them be unknown. There is one more rule about keys. They appear in addresses, in plans and in state, in plain sight. That is why Terraform refuses to use a sensitive value as a for each key, as the second error shows.

Here is the same set of three web config files, built two different ways. With count, each instance is identified by its position in a list: web zero, web one, web two. With for each, each instance is identified by a key: web a, web b, web c. Both work fine on day one. The difference shows up when the list changes. Remove web a, the first item, and plan again. With count, every index after the removed one shifts down by one. Instance zero, which used to be web a, now has to become web b, and instance one has to become web c. For these files a new filename forces replacement, so the plan replaces two instances and destroys the third: two to add, three to destroy, to remove one file. With for each, the plan is exactly what you meant. web a is destroyed, and nothing else is touched, because the other keys did not change. That is the whole lesson: state binds addresses to objects, and with count the address is a position, so positions moving means objects churning. Use count for genuinely identical copies, or for switching a single resource on and off. Use for each whenever your instances have names.

Every instance in a plan gets one action, and the symbols on the left are the complete list. Create, update in place, replace in either order, destroy, and read for data sources. How does Terraform choose? It compares the configuration with the state, and then it asks the provider. The provider's schema says, for every argument, whether it can be changed on an existing object. Some cannot. Change one of those and the only way to get there is a new object, and the plan marks the argument with forces replacement. Look at the real plan. Two variables changed. terraform data's input can be updated in place, so the release keeps its ID and gets a tilde. The local file's content cannot be changed in place, so the file must be replaced, and the symbol is minus slash plus. Take replacement seriously. It is not an update. It is a new object with a new ID, so anything that referred to the old one may have to change too, and by default the old object is destroyed before its replacement is created. The last two cases are simple: an instance in state but no longer in configuration is destroyed, and one in configuration but not in state is created.

Sometimes the default behaviour is not what you want, and a lifecycle block lets you change it for one resource. There are four rules, and each card on the left is a real run. create before destroy flips the replacement order: the new object is created first, then the old one is removed, which avoids a gap. But look at the top left. The new file had the same name as the old one, apply reported success, and then destroying the old object deleted the file that had just been written. Create first only works when old and new can exist side by side, which usually means unique names. prevent destroy makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail. That is useful protection, with a limit: the rule lives inside the resource block, so if someone deletes the whole block, the protection goes with it and the destroy goes ahead. ignore changes tells Terraform to stop diffing the listed arguments, which is how you share an argument with another tool. The cost: the configuration says two point oh, the object holds one point oh, and the plan says no changes. And replace triggered by replaces this resource whenever another one changes, here replacing the web file because the release was updated.

Not everything you need fits neatly into a resource's arguments, and Terraform has a few escape hatches for those cases. The first is the one we have been using all along: terraform data. Besides holding values, it has triggers replace, which replaces it whenever the listed values change. Combine that with a provisioner and you can run a command, here a schema migration script, each time the database configuration changes. But be honest about what you lose. The plan can say that the command will run. It cannot say what the command will do, whether it will succeed, or whether running it twice is safe. That is why the documentation calls provisioners a last resort, behind a provider feature or a tool built for deployment. Timeouts are a different kind of setting. They let slow operations, like creating a database, take longer, but they are defined by each provider, per resource and per operation. Here create and delete validate, and an invented resize argument is rejected. And finally dash target, which plans only part of the configuration. The warning on the left is Terraform's own advice: it is for recovering from errors, not for routine deployment.

Let's finish the chapter with the case every plan is silent about: what happens when apply fails partway through. Here the plan was three resources: the web file, the database file, and the migration. Both files were created. Then the migration script failed, and apply stopped with an error. Now the important part. Nothing was rolled back. Terraform apply is not a transaction. The two files exist, they are recorded in state, and they stay. Terraform cannot undo real-world changes in general, so it does not try. The resource that failed is marked tainted, which means the next plan will replace it rather than trust it. So recovery means: understand and fix the cause, then plan again. That new plan starts from what actually exists now, not from what you hoped would exist. Saved plans play a part here too. Applying a saved plan file carries out exactly the actions that were reviewed. But if anything changed the state after the plan was made, including another apply, the saved plan no longer describes reality, and Terraform refuses to apply it, as the card on the right shows. Reviewed intent stays tied to the state it was reviewed against. Chapter four is about protecting that state.

Chapter one introduced state as Terraform's record. This chapter is about protecting that record, so let's look inside it first. On the left is a real state file, trimmed to one resource. The most important part is the binding: the address terraform data dot release is tied to one particular object, identified by its ID. Alongside the binding sit the attributes, the values Terraform observed the last time it refreshed or applied, and the outputs. Then there is metadata. The serial number increases as the state is rewritten, and the lineage identifies this state's history, so Terraform can tell one snapshot from another and refuse to mix them up. One rule follows from all of this: every real object should be owned by exactly one state. If two states both believe they manage the same object, each apply undoes the other's work, and neither plan warns you. Finally, read state through commands, terraform state list and terraform state show, rather than opening the JSON. And never edit it by hand. When state genuinely needs changing, chapter six covers the tools built for that.

Real infrastructure does not stay still just because Terraform is not running. Someone edits a setting in a console, a script changes a file, and now the state's record no longer matches reality. That difference is called drift. Terraform finds it through refresh. Before planning, it asks the provider to read every object again and compares what it sees with what state recorded. Notice something on the left. Someone changed the config file by hand, and the local file provider reports it as deleted, not as changed. That is a real detail of this provider: it compares checksums, and a mismatch means the object it created is gone. What drift looks like is always the provider's decision. Once drift is found, you have two possible answers. A refresh-only plan accepts reality: applying it updates the record and changes nothing real. A normal plan does the opposite: it puts the object back the way the configuration says, here by writing port eight thousand eighty again. Terraform will not choose for you, and neither answer is always right. Decide which side is correct, the change someone made or the configuration, before you apply either plan.

Two questions are easy to blur together. Where is the state stored? And where do plan and apply actually run? The backend answers the first one only. With the default local backend, state is a file next to your configuration. That is fine for learning, but the state exists on one disk, and nobody else can safely use it. Move to a remote backend, like S3, and the state becomes an object in a bucket that a team can share and lock. But look at the lock information on the left, captured while an apply was running against that bucket. The path is in the bucket. The who is the machine the command was typed on. The state moved; the execution did not. Plans still run on your laptop, or on a CI runner, with that machine's credentials. Remote execution is a different feature. HCP Terraform, for example, can run plans and applies on its own runners, or it can store state while runs stay local. Keep the two decisions separate, because the second one decides where your cloud credentials have to live.

A backend is configured with a backend block inside the terraform block. Here it names a bucket, a key for this configuration's state, a region, and two settings worth keeping: native locking with a lock file, and encryption. Before any of this works, there is a bootstrap problem. The bucket has to exist before Terraform can store state in it, so it is usually created separately, by hand or by a small configuration of its own. And backend settings are read before variables exist, so they cannot use variables. Values that differ per environment go in backend config files passed to init instead. Changing the backend always means running init again, and Terraform says so if you forget. When state already exists, init dash migrate-state offers to copy it to the new backend, and asks first, as you can see. After migrating, run a plan. It should report no changes, because the record moved and reality did not. Then clean up. The migration left behind an empty state file and a backup that still contains the entire old state, secrets included. And the dot terraform folder remembers backend settings, which is one more reason never to pass credentials as backend config.

State is a single shared record, and two people writing it at once is the classic way to lose work. On the left, writer A starts an apply against the S3 backend. A few seconds later, writer B tries to apply too. B fails immediately, before touching anything, and the lock information says who holds the lock and what they are doing. That failure is the lock working. Now the same race with locking switched off. A changes the release, B changes the port. Both applies report apply complete. But each one started from the same snapshot and wrote back its own version of the whole state, and A wrote last. The result: the file on disk says port nine thousand ninety, because B really did change it, while the state still records port eight thousand eighty, because A's snapshot never knew about B's change. Both commands succeeded, and the record is now wrong, so the next plan works from a false picture. Locking is a backend feature. Local state and S3 with use lockfile both lock, but not every backend does, so check before you share one. And treat dash lock equals false, and force-unlock, as emergency tools.

State deserves two kinds of protection at once. It holds every attribute of every resource, including passwords and keys, so it needs protecting like a credential. And it holds the only record of which objects Terraform owns, so it needs protecting like a database. The bucket on the left does both. Objects are encrypted at rest, and versioning is switched on, so every write the chapter's runs made is still there, all the way back to the original migrated copy. If a bad apply or a lost update corrupts the record, a previous version can be restored. Access is the third control: only a few roles should be able to read state, and fewer still should be able to write it. Then there are copies, and they escape easily. A dot backup file left by a migration, the output of terraform state pull, a saved plan, an artifact kept by a CI job: each holds the same secrets as the state itself, and each needs the same protection or deleting. One limit to remember. An old version of state is only an old record. Restoring it does not bring back an object or data that was destroyed, and chapter ten deals with that properly.

So far each example has been one root module with one state. Larger systems are usually split into several, and the reason is blast radius. Here the network and the application are separate root modules, with separate state files. Each one plans, locks and fails on its own. A mistake in the application's configuration cannot produce a plan that destroys the network, because the network is simply not in that state. The cost of splitting is that the parts still depend on each other, and the dependency has to be made explicit. terraform remote state is the built-in way: the application reads the network's outputs, here the network's address range, and carves a subnet from it. But look at the bottom card. To read those outputs, the reader needs read access to the entire network state, not just the outputs. With that same access, the whole file is readable, including a note that was never published as an output. That is why the documentation suggests alternatives for sharing values between states: publishing them somewhere designed for it, or looking up the real objects with a data source.

CLI workspaces let one configuration keep several states. terraform workspace new staging creates an empty state alongside the default one, and in the S3 backend it appears under an env colon slash staging prefix in the same bucket. Inside the configuration, terraform dot workspace returns the current name, so resources can be named per workspace. That sounds like environments, and it is often used that way, so be clear about what is and is not separated. Only the state is. The code is the same code. The backend is the same bucket. And the credentials that can write staging's state can write production's, because they are the same credentials. Nothing stops the wrong apply except remembering which workspace is selected. For environments that need real isolation, use separate root directories or separate backends, each with its own credentials and access policy, so a staging pipeline physically cannot touch production. One naming warning to finish. HCP Terraform also has workspaces, but they are a different, much heavier concept, each with its own settings, permissions and variables. Same word, different thing.

Every configuration so far has been a single module: the root module, the directory you run Terraform in. Now we split code out into a child module. A child module is just another directory of dot t f files, and the root calls it with a module block. The source argument says where the code lives, here a local folder, and terraform init installs it. The other arguments set the child's input variables, and the root reads the child's outputs with expressions like module dot web dot config path. Here is the part to slow down for. Moving a resource into a module changes its address. What was local file dot web config is now module dot web dot local file dot config. Terraform binds state to addresses, so a new address looks like a new resource, and the plan on the left proposes to destroy the old file and create a new one, even though nothing about the file changed. Chapter six shows how a moved block tells Terraform the two addresses are the same object. And remember: a child module's resources live in the caller's state. A module organises code. It does not create a separate state or a separate permission boundary.

A module's interface is its variables and its outputs, and nothing else. Callers should never need to know which resources are inside. So treat the interface as a contract. Every variable gets a type and a description. Where a value has rules, write them down as a validation block: here, the port must be between ten twenty-four and sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-five. Then look at what happens when a caller passes port eighty. The error points at the caller's own line, shows the value it passed, prints the message the module author wrote, and names the rule that rejected it. The caller learns the contract without opening the module's code. Defaults deserve care too. A default is a decision made on behalf of every caller, so add one only where a single value really does suit almost everyone, and leave the rest required. Outputs work the same way in reverse. Expose what callers actually need, not every attribute you happen to have, and describe each one, because once a caller depends on an output, renaming or removing it is a breaking change.

Where a module comes from is set by its source argument, and each kind of source is versioned differently. A local path, like dot slash modules slash web, has no version of its own: it changes whenever the repository changes, which is ideal for modules that live alongside the configuration using them. A registry source names a published module, and a separate version argument selects a release with the same constraint syntax you use for providers. A Git source points at a repository, and the ref parameter pins a tag or commit. On the left, a Git source pinned to v one point oh point oh is installed by init into the dot terraform slash modules folder. Notice the last line, too: the module asks for local version two point nine or newer, the root asks for tilde greater-than two point nine, and Terraform combines both ranges. Changing a source or a version means running init again. And one important gap: the dependency lock file records providers only. Modules are never locked, so the only protection is pinning them explicitly and reviewing every upgrade as you would any code change.

Modules need providers, and the rule is that the caller supplies them. In the simple case you write nothing at all: a child module automatically uses the caller's default configuration of each provider. That is why reusable modules should not contain provider blocks of their own. A module that hard-codes a region or an account can only ever be used in that region and that account. Sometimes a module genuinely needs more than one configuration, like this bucket module, which creates a primary bucket and a replica somewhere else. It says so in its required providers block, with configuration aliases: it expects a second AWS configuration that it calls aws dot replica. The caller then decides which of its own configurations to hand over, in the providers argument. Here the replica gets the d r alias, in us west two, and the plan places one bucket in each region. Leave that mapping out and Terraform refuses, naming the alias the module expected. Keeping this decision with the caller is the point: regions, accounts and credentials are deployment choices, and the same module code can serve every environment.

Once you have several modules, the question is how they fit together. A tempting design is for each module to create everything it needs: an app module that builds its own network, its own database, its own everything. That module works exactly once, in exactly one situation. The alternative is composition. Keep modules small, and wire them together in the root. Here the app module asks for a network as an input, an object with an ID and an address range, and it never creates one. Its caller decides where that network comes from. The first caller passes the output of a network module. The second passes a network that already existed, created by another team long ago, using literal values. The same app module serves both, unchanged. This is called dependency inversion: the module depends on an interface, not on a particular implementation. It also keeps the dependency visible, as a reference in the root configuration, where anyone reading it can see what connects to what. And notice how the input is shaped: it asks for only the two values the app actually uses, not the network's every attribute.

The for each and count arguments from chapter three work on module blocks as well, so one call can create several complete instances of a module. Here the services variable maps names to ports, and the service module is called once for each entry. Every resource inside gets an address that includes the key: module dot service, open bracket, api, and module dot service, web. Everything chapter three said about keys applies. Use stable names rather than positions, and make sure the keys are known at plan time. Outputs need one more step. Because the module has several instances, module dot service is no longer a single object. It is a map of instances, keyed exactly like the for each. Callers rarely want that raw shape, so a for expression reshapes it, here into one map from each service name to its config path, which is what the output shows after apply. One design rule to finish. Repeat a module for many instances of the same kind of thing. If two instances need very different settings, they are probably different things, and they deserve their own module blocks.

Not every module is worth writing. The test is simple: a module earns its place when its interface is smaller than the thing it hides. Here are two modules for the same bucket, called with the same typo, versioning spelled without its second n. The first is an over-general wrapper. It takes a single settings input of type any and looks keys up inside it. Because any accepts anything, the misspelled key is simply never read. The plan is accepted, versioning is false, and nobody is told. Wrappers like this also force every caller to read the module's source to discover which keys exist, so the interface hides nothing at all. The second is a narrow module with one typed variable per input and a default that encodes a decision, versioning on. The same typo is an unsupported argument, and Terraform even suggests the right name. Narrow modules also need looking after. Give each one a README and an example call, publish it with versions, and change its interface rarely and deliberately, because every change to an interface is a change for every caller.

So far Terraform has created everything it manages. Real systems rarely start that way. There are servers, buckets and networks that someone built by hand, or with another tool, and at some point you want Terraform to manage them. That is called adoption, and it starts with questions rather than commands. What exists, and who created it? Who should own it from now on, meaning which state and which root module? Is any other tool still changing it, because if so, you will be fighting that tool on every apply. Then there is a technical question: can this resource type be imported at all? That is the provider's decision, per resource type. On the left, an import of a local file is refused outright: the provider simply has not implemented it. The random integer resource can be imported, and so can an S3 bucket, and each type defines its own format for the import ID, which you will find in the provider's documentation. And keep one limit in mind for the whole chapter. Importing an object records it in state. It does not mean the object is configured the way you want.

Terraform's modern way to adopt an object is an import block, written in configuration and reviewed like everything else. It has two arguments. to is the address the object will be bound to, here random integer dot port. id is the provider's identifier for the existing object, and its format belongs to the provider. For a random integer it is three numbers: the result, the minimum and the maximum. Run a plan and the import appears alongside the usual changes, one to import, and nothing happens until apply. Now look at the two plans on the left, because the second one is a genuine mistake made while preparing this course. The ID was written with its fields in the wrong order. Terraform did not complain. The provider accepted it and planned to adopt an object whose minimum is larger than its maximum. That is the lesson: an import ID is only checked by the provider, and only as far as the provider chooses to check it. So read the imported values in the plan as carefully as you would read a destroy. Nothing else will tell you that you adopted the wrong thing.

An import block needs configuration to go with it, a resource block at the destination address. For one object you can write it by hand. For many, Terraform can draft it: run plan with the generate config out option, and it writes a resource block for each import, filled in from the object it found. On the left is the result for our random integer. Every argument is spelled out, with null for anything not set. And notice the warning printed alongside: configuration generation is still experimental, and its format may change. Generated configuration is a starting point, because it cannot know your intentions. It does not know which values should come from variables or references to other resources, so everything arrives as a literal. It cannot tell a value you chose from one that merely happens to match a default. And if the object holds a secret, that secret is now sitting in a file, about to be committed. So review it like any other change: drop the noise, replace literals with references, check for secrets, move the block into the file where it belongs, and then plan again.

Applying the plan imports the object, and the summary says so: one imported. The object is now bound in state. But the job is not finished, because the configuration and the object still have to agree, and the way to check is the next plan. The goal of reconciliation is a plan that says no changes. Here, tidying the generated block by removing its null arguments made no difference, which is what you want. But then the maximum was edited to eight thousand ninety-nine, perhaps to match some convention, and the plan proposed to replace the object, because that argument cannot change in place. Replacing an object you just went to the trouble of adopting is usually the opposite of what you intended. So read every post-import diff with care. An update changes a real system that, until a moment ago, nobody was managing with Terraform. A replacement destroys it. For each difference, decide which side is right, the configuration or the object, and change the configuration until the plan is empty. Once applied, the import block has done its job. You can delete it, or keep it as a record.

Chapter five ended with a problem. Extracting a resource into a module changed its address, and Terraform planned to destroy the object and create it again. The fix is a moved block. It says, in configuration, that an object which used to live at one address now lives at another. Here there are two: a rename, from api config to api, and the module extraction, from local file dot web config to module dot web dot local file dot config. Look at the plan. Instead of destroy and create, each resource has moved, the ID on the new address is the same ID as before, and the summary is zero to add, zero to change, zero to destroy. The same mechanism handles moves between count, for each and single instances, which is how you fix the count problem from chapter three without churning anything. Moved blocks are cheap to keep and costly to delete too early. Another workspace, or a teammate's copy, may not have applied the move yet. And if you publish a module, keep old moved blocks indefinitely, because every caller upgrading from an older version needs them.

Sometimes the right change is for Terraform to stop managing an object, without destroying it. Perhaps it is moving to another team's configuration, or being retired from automation. Simply deleting the resource block does not do that. As the first plan shows, an object in state but not in configuration is destroyed. A removed block expresses the other intention. It names the address and, with destroy set to false, tells Terraform to forget the object instead. The plan says the object will no longer be managed, but will not be destroyed, warns you about it, and after apply the file is still on disk. Only the binding in state went away. This is also how you hand ownership between two configurations safely. The old owner applies a removed block with destroy false. The new owner then applies an import block for the same object. Doing it in that order means there is never a moment when two states both believe they own it. One caution: between those two steps, and forever if no one imports it, nobody is watching the object. Any drift goes unnoticed until someone adopts it again.

Everything so far in this chapter has gone through a plan you can review. The terraform state commands do not. They edit bindings in state directly, immediately, and they are the right tool only for what the blocks cannot express. state mv rebinds an object to a new address, and dash dry run shows what it would do first. state rm forgets a binding, the same effect as a removed block, but without any plan or review. Notice that on local state each command leaves a timestamped backup file behind, which is useful and, as chapter four said, one more copy of the state to protect. state mv can also move a binding into a different local state file, with dash state out. For remote states the recommended route is the one from the previous section: a removed block in the old configuration, and an import block in the new one, each planned and reviewed. Before any state surgery, stop every other writer and make sure you hold the lock, and pull a copy of the state to a file, so that if something goes wrong you can put it back. Chapter ten returns to that kind of recovery.

This chapter is about evidence: what can each kind of check actually prove? We start with the cheapest. terraform fmt checks layout, and terraform validate checks the configuration against the language and the providers' schemas, all without touching any real system. On the left is a configuration with three mistakes. validate catches two of them: an argument that is not in the resource's schema, and a file permission that is not valid octal, which the provider's own schema validation rejects. Fix those two and validate says success. But the third mistake is still there. The second file points at a directory that cannot be created, and only the real system knows that. So apply creates the first file, then fails on the second. That is the boundary of static checks. They cannot know about paths, quotas, permissions, names already taken, or anything else that only the real system can answer. And they certainly cannot tell whether the configuration does what you intended. Run them anyway, on every save and every commit, because they cost seconds and catch a lot. Just treat a clean validate as the floor, not as evidence that a change is safe.

A validation block turns a rule about an input into an error, and the error appears before any planning starts, which is the cheapest possible moment to find out. Most rules check a single variable: a range, a format, a list of allowed values, with functions like can and regex for things like names and address ranges. Rules can also look at more than one variable. Here the instance count rule reads the environment too: production needs at least two instances for redundancy. Passing environment prod with one instance fails immediately, and look at how much the error tells you. Terraform shows both variables' values and points at the rule. Then comes the message the author wrote, and that is where most rules fall short. A good message says what the rule is, why it exists, and what value was actually received. Got one beats invalid input every time, because the caller can fix the problem without opening the module. What validation cannot do is look at real objects. It only sees inputs. For rules about what exists or what was created, you need conditions, which are next.

Validation checks inputs. Conditions check real values, and there are three kinds. A precondition, inside a resource's lifecycle block, states an assumption that must hold before that resource changes. A postcondition states a guarantee about the result, using self to refer to the resource's own attributes. Both are errors, and both stop anything that depends on them. The subtle part is timing. Conditions run as early as their values are known. The postcondition on the left checks the file's permissions, which are known during planning, so it failed at plan, before anything was created. The precondition checks a randomly generated port, which does not exist until apply. So apply created the random number first, and only then did the precondition fail and block the file. That is chapter three's lesson again: a failure partway through apply leaves what already succeeded in place. The third kind is the check block, which sits outside any resource and makes assertions about the configuration as a whole. A failing check is only a warning. Notice that apply completed anyway. Check blocks report problems. They never stop anything.

terraform test runs a module against inputs you choose and checks the results with assertions. Tests live in files ending dot t f test dot h c l, next to the module. On the left is a test file for chapter five's web module. A top-level variables block sets the inputs for every run. Each run block is one plan or apply, followed by its assertions. The first run plans with the default port and asserts the rendered content. The second passes port eighty and uses expect failures: it passes only if the port validation rule rejects the input, which is how you test that your rules actually work. The third run has no command, and that matters, because the default command is apply. That run created a real file, checked that it existed, and then Terraform destroyed it again when the test file finished. Plan runs create nothing at all, so prefer them wherever a plan can answer the question. When an assertion fails, Terraform shows the actual and expected values as a diff, here eight thousand eighty against nine thousand ninety. The remaining runs still execute, and the file as a whole is marked as failed.

Apply tests create real objects, which can be slow, costly and impossible without credentials. A mock provider is the alternative. Declare mock provider in a test file and every resource from that provider is simulated: nothing is created, no credentials are needed, and computed attributes get generated values. When a test needs particular values, override resource and override data pin them. That makes mocks excellent for testing a module's own logic: its expressions, its conditionals, its outputs, quickly and on every change. But look at what happens on the left. The same run, writing a file into a directory that cannot exist, appears in two test files. With the mock provider, it passes. Against the real provider, it fails, because the real system refuses. Neither result is wrong. They answer different questions. The mocked run proves the module's logic produced the path it should. Only the real run can show whether the real system accepts it, along with quotas, permissions, naming rules and provider bugs. So use both: mocks for logic on every change, and real apply tests before a release.

By now there are many kinds of check, and the useful question is not which one is best, but which claim you need to support. The table on the left matches claims to evidence. That the syntax and schema are valid: fmt and validate. That inputs meet the contract: validation rules and conditions. That the plan has the right shape, or that the module's logic holds: plan runs and mocked tests, none of which create anything. That the real API accepts the configuration: only an apply, ideally in a separate test account. Some claims sit outside Terraform entirely. Policy checks evaluate a plan against organisational rules, such as no publicly readable buckets, and chapter nine comes back to how they are enforced. Security scanners look for risky settings in the configuration. And the claim that the system actually works, that users can reach it and it behaves correctly, needs health checks and monitoring against the running system, which no Terraform test can replace. Then order the checks by cost: the cheapest on every save, plan tests and policy on every change, and slow, real apply tests before a release.

Let's finish the chapter with the limits of the evidence itself. A passing test proves what it asserted, under the conditions it ran in, and nothing more. Look at this run. The assertion passed. Then, during teardown, the resource's destroy step failed, here a queue that still held messages, and Terraform could not remove it. The test file is marked as failed even though every run passed, and Terraform lists exactly which resources were left behind and must be cleaned up by hand. With a real cloud provider, those leftovers keep running, and keep costing money, until someone notices. That is why apply tests belong in an isolated account, never in production, and why teams that run them usually add a regular sweeper job to remove anything left over. Apply tests are also slow and cost money on every run, which is another reason to keep them for the questions that genuinely need them. And remember what no test proves. It does not show that production, with its real data and real traffic, will behave the same way. And it does not show that the next provider release will still pass, which is why tests run again on every upgrade.

Security in Terraform starts with a simple question: who is acting? In one apply there are usually four identities. People write code and review plans. A CI runner actually executes plan and apply on their behalf. The provider uses credentials to call the cloud API, and the backend uses credentials to read and write state. These are often the same set of all-powerful keys, and they should not be. The table on the left is a reasonable starting point. A person, day to day, can read plans but does not apply directly. A CI job that only plans can read state and take the lock, but changes nothing. A CI job that applies can write state and change infrastructure, for one environment only. Notice that the backend and the infrastructure can use different credentials entirely, so the identity that writes state need not be the identity that can delete databases. And people still need a way in for emergencies. That is a break-glass role: used rarely, logged every time, and reviewed afterwards, rather than everyday administrator access that nobody remembers having.

The classic way to give CI access to a cloud is to create access keys and paste them into the CI system's secret settings. Those keys never expire, they get copied into other jobs, and when they leak, they keep working until someone notices. Federation removes them. Modern CI systems can issue a signed identity token for each run, stating which repository and which branch the job comes from. The cloud account has a trust policy that accepts tokens only from that repository and that branch, and in exchange it issues temporary credentials that expire, here within an hour. In Terraform, the AWS provider does the exchange itself, with an assume role with web identity block naming the role, the token file and a session name. The configuration on the left validates against the real provider, and notice what it does not contain: any secret at all. The weak point moves to the trust policy, so write it carefully. If it accepts any branch, or tokens from forks of the repository, then anyone who can push a branch can apply to your infrastructure.

Chapter two showed a sensitive output being redacted. This chapter is about the limits of that. Marking a variable sensitive changes how Terraform displays it. In the plan on the left, the password appears as sensitive value, while the user name beside it is shown in full. The marking also spreads: anything computed from a sensitive value is treated as sensitive too, and a root output built from one must itself be marked sensitive, or Terraform refuses. What sensitive does not do is just as important. It does not encrypt the value. It does not keep it out of state. And it does not hide it from machine-readable output, such as terraform output dash json or the JSON form of a plan, which tools read for exactly that reason. Removing the marking is deliberately explicit. The nonsensitive function strips it, and the console shows the password in plain text. Sometimes that is legitimate, such as a value that only looks secret. But every use of nonsensitive deserves review, because it is precisely how a secret ends up printed in a CI log.

So where does a sensitive value actually end up? The scene on the left is the result of searching for one after a single plan with dash out and a single apply. The state contains it twice, in plain text, once in the input and once in the output. The saved plan file looks clean, but only because it is a compressed archive that grep cannot read. Ask Terraform for its JSON form and there is the password. The trace-level debug log from this run did not contain it, but that is a property of this provider and this run, not a guarantee. Providers can and do log request bodies. So treat every artefact as holding the secret. State, saved plans and plan JSON need the protection chapter four described. Pipeline artefacts deserve particular attention, because CI systems keep them, often for weeks, and often with broad read access. Keep saved plans short-lived and in restricted storage, delete them after apply, and never turn on debug logging in a shared CI log. And remember the dot terraform folder keeps backend settings you passed to init, so credentials never belong there either.

Sensitive values are hidden from display but stored. Ephemeral values are the other approach: they exist only while Terraform is running and are never written to state or to a plan file. A value becomes ephemeral in two ways. A variable can be declared ephemeral, and providers offer ephemeral resources, such as a random password generated fresh on every run. Then there are rules about where an ephemeral value may go. Provider configuration and provisioners are allowed, and on the left a migration provisioner uses the password, after which the state and the plan contain no trace of it. An ordinary resource argument is not allowed, because its value must be stored, and Terraform refuses with the error you can see. For resources, providers add write-only arguments. A database's password write-only argument accepts an ephemeral value, sends it to the API and never stores it. The plan simply says write-only attribute. There are costs. An ephemeral variable set at plan must be supplied again at apply. Terraform cannot see a write-only value change, so you bump a version number to rotate it. And write-only arguments exist only where a provider has added them.

Every terraform init downloads code: the providers, the modules, and before that the Terraform binary itself. That code then runs with your cloud credentials, so each download needs two things: a pin, so you get the same thing every time, and a check, so you know it is what it claims to be. For providers, version constraints choose a version and the lock file pins it, along with checksums of the package. On the left, one recorded checksum was changed, and init refused to install the provider, because the package no longer matches what the team reviewed and committed. That is the lock file doing its job. Modules are weaker. Pin them to a registry version or, better for Git sources, a specific commit. But nothing hashes module code the way providers are hashed, so the only real check is reviewing the code when you upgrade. And the CLI itself: pin the version your pipelines use, and verify the download against the published checksums and their signature, which is exactly how the Terraform binary used for this course was checked. Finally, the cheapest control of all: fewer dependencies, from sources you know.

Least privilege means each identity gets only the actions its job needs, on only the resources its environment owns. On the left is a policy for a staging plan role, written as a Terraform policy document and rendered as JSON. It can read one object, the staging state. It can list only the staging prefix of the bucket. And there is one statement that is easy to miss: with S3 native locking, even a plan writes and deletes a small lock file, so a role that can only read will fail to take the lock. Granting put and delete on that one lock object, and nothing else, keeps the role honest. The same thinking scales up. Give each environment its own apply role, so a staging pipeline cannot change production. Put production in its own account, with its own state, as chapter four suggested. And keep these policies as code, reviewed like any other change, because a quiet edit to a policy is as significant as an edit to infrastructure. Start narrow. When a permission is genuinely missing, the error names the denied action, and you add exactly that one.

This chapter puts everything so far into a team workflow, and it starts with version control. Infrastructure changes should travel exactly like application code: on a branch, through a review, into a merge, leaving a history you can read later. On the left is the repository used for every run in this chapter. There is one module, with its tests beside it, and one root module per environment, staging and production. The lock files are committed, and state, saved plans and the dot terraform folders are ignored, for the reasons chapters two, four and eight gave. The pipeline scripts live in the same repository as the code they check. Ownership is expressed in a code owners file, which most Git hosts read to route reviews by path. Changes to shared modules go to the platform team, and changes under the production directory need production approvers. Then the review itself has three questions. Intent: is this the change we actually want? Plan: is this what will actually happen? A diff of configuration does not answer that; the plan does. And owner: is the person approving the right one for this part of the system?

Reviewers should not have to guess what a change will do, so every pull request runs the same checks automatically, cheapest first. The script on the left is the one used in this chapter, and below it is a real run against staging. First fmt dash check, which fails if anything is not in canonical layout. Then the module's own tests, all three passing. Then validate for the environment, and finally a plan. Notice the dash input equals false on every command. In CI there is nobody to answer a prompt, so a missing variable must fail immediately rather than hang until the job times out. That last plan is called a speculative plan. It shows what would happen if this branch were merged and applied right now, and its output is posted to the review so reviewers read the real consequences. It is never applied by the pull request job itself. But it is saved with dash out, because, as the next section shows, applying exactly that file is how the reviewed change and the applied change stay the same. And plan jobs should run with the plan-only role from chapter eight: they read state and take the lock, and nothing more.

Here is the gap that saved plans close. Reviewers approved a plan that changes staging's port from eight thousand eighty to nine thousand ninety. Before anyone applied it, an unrelated pull request merged and set the port to seven thousand seventy. Now someone runs terraform apply without a plan file. Terraform plans again, from the files as they are now, and proposes seven thousand seventy, a change that no reviewer ever saw. Here it was cancelled. Instead, apply the saved plan file. Terraform carries out exactly the reviewed actions, and the file on disk now says nine thousand ninety. The configuration still says seven thousand seventy, of course, so the next plan shows that as a change of its own, which goes through its own review. That is the property you want: what was approved is what was applied, and nothing else slips in alongside it. Saved plans have a freshness rule too. If the state changes after the plan is made, chapter three showed Terraform refusing the stale file. So apply soon after approval, and if too much time has passed, plan again and review again.

Production changes should not be the first time a change has ever been applied anywhere. Promotion means a change passes through staging first, gets applied there, is observed working, and only then moves to production. In this repository that is literally visible. Staging was changed and applied earlier. The promotion commit changes production's value, and both environments are planned. Staging reports no changes, because it already has the new port. Production shows the same change it is about to receive, for its own approval. Promotion also needs ordering. Two merges landing close together must not race to apply the same state, so CI queues runs per environment, not per branch, and each plan and apply waits for the state lock instead of failing immediately, which is what the five-minute lock timeout in the CI script does. Concurrent merges then reach apply one after another, each against the state the previous one left. One design note: promote versions, not copies. Each environment should pin a module version, so moving production forward is a one-line change. Copy-pasted environment directories slowly drift away from each other.

Drift happens between applies, so the only way to notice it promptly is to look on a schedule. A nightly job plans each environment and never applies anything. The useful flag is dash detailed exit code. With it, plan exits with zero when there is nothing to do, two when it found changes, and one when something went wrong, which is easy for a scheduler to act on. But a normal plan's two mixes together two very different situations, and this chapter's environments show both. Staging has no drift at all. It has a merged change that nobody applied. Production has real drift: someone edited the file by hand. Both return two. A refresh-only plan separates them, because it only compares state with reality and ignores the configuration, so the script runs both and reports two numbers. Staging: drift zero, pending two. Production: drift two. Each signal should go to someone. Drift goes to the owner, who decides, as chapter four described, whether the manual change should stay or be reverted. Pending changes go back through the normal path of review and controlled apply.

Some rules apply to every change, whoever writes it: no world-writable files, no public storage buckets, no instance types above a certain size, required tags on everything. Writing those as policy turns them into checks that run against the plan, before anything is applied. The mechanism is simple. terraform show dash json turns a saved plan into structured data, and a policy engine reads it. Real teams use tools such as Open Policy Agent or Sentinel. On the left is a deliberately tiny stand-in, a Python script with one rule, and run against staging's saved plan it finds the default world-writable permission and exits with a failure. The important question is where the check runs, because that decides what it can actually stop. A comment on the review is advice that can be ignored. A required check blocks merging, until an administrator overrides it. A check in the apply pipeline stops only the applies that go through that pipeline. Only the cloud's own permissions stop every route, including someone running apply from a laptop. Cost belongs here too: estimating each plan's monthly cost and flagging large jumps catches expensive mistakes during review.

Everything this chapter has built by hand, a run queue per environment, stored plans, approvals, policy checks, drift detection and an audit trail, also comes bundled in HashiCorp's hosted service, HCP Terraform, and its self-hosted form, Terraform Enterprise. A cloud block in the terraform block connects a configuration to it, naming an organisation and a workspace. That block is shown here for comparison only. It was not run, and nothing in this course requires a commercial service. The name workspace causes real confusion, so compare the two carefully. A CLI workspace, from chapter four, is one extra state for the same configuration, and nothing more: the same backend, the same credentials, no access control of its own. An HCP workspace is much larger. It has its own state, its own variables and stored credentials, its own team permissions, a queue of runs and their history. It can run plans and applies on HashiCorp's infrastructure, or in local mode where it only stores state. Some features depend on the edition and plan you have. When you compare it with a self-built pipeline, compare against the same list of needs this chapter covered.

Sooner or later someone will ask about a change that happened months ago. What exactly changed? Who approved it? Which code and which tools produced it? The answers are cheap to record at apply time and nearly impossible to reconstruct later. On the left is a provenance record for the production apply in this chapter, assembled from real commands: the Git commit, the Terraform version, the provider version from the lock file, a hash of the exact plan file that was applied, and a summary of the actions in it. Add who approved and which identity ran it, plus the apply log and outputs, and you can answer the auditor's questions. Store these records somewhere the pipeline itself cannot rewrite, so the evidence survives even if the pipeline is compromised. And keep secrets out of them: store summaries and hashes, not the plan files themselves, which as chapter eight showed contain secret values. Distributing modules belongs to the same story. Tag each release, have callers pin the tag, and keep a changelog that says what each version changes, so an upgrade can be reviewed as carefully as any other change.

The last chapter is about what happens when things go wrong, and what happens as systems grow. It starts with diagnosis. Almost every Terraform error names the layer that failed in its first line, and the table on the left collects the ones you have already met in this course. A configuration error, like an unsupported argument, is your code, and validate usually finds it. A provider error, like an import that is not implemented, is about what a resource type supports. Credential and network errors mean Terraform never reached the API at all. The example here is genuine: the machine that produced this course cannot reach the public registry, and this is exactly what that looks like. State errors are about locks, serial numbers and lineage, which the next sections cover. And quota or API errors mean the remote system received the request and refused it. To narrow a problem down, reproduce it with the smallest command that fails, change one thing at a time, and plan after each change. Debug logging shows the actual requests, but keep it out of shared logs. And when the failure is inside a provider or the API itself, escalate rather than working around it.

Chapter three showed an apply that failed. This is an apply that was interrupted, by someone pressing control C in the middle of a twenty-second database migration. Terraform does not just stop. It says interrupt received, asks you to wait, and shuts down gracefully, finishing what it can record. The web config file had already been created, and it is in state. The migration was killed six seconds in. The API file was never started. Recovery begins with observation, not action. List what state recorded, look at the real objects, and make a fresh plan. Here the plan proposes creating the API file and replacing the migration, which is marked tainted because it did not finish. But notice what the plan cannot tell you. A migration that was killed halfway may already have changed the database schema, or part of it. Running it again is only safe if it is written to be idempotent, so that a second run finishes the work instead of failing or doing it twice. That is a question about your system, not about Terraform. One more thing: a second control C kills Terraform outright, without recording anything. Avoid it.

When state itself goes wrong, Terraform has safeguards, and it is worth knowing both what they protect and what overriding them costs. terraform state push refuses an older serial number over a newer state, and refuses a state from a different lineage, because both usually mean someone is about to overwrite newer work with the wrong file. You can force past both. Here, a backup taken before a database file was destroyed was pushed back with dash force. State now lists the database again. But the data directory is empty, and the next plan wants to create it. Restoring state restores the record, never the object or its data. For a real database, that would be a new, empty database. Recovering the data is a backup and restore problem for the database, not a Terraform problem. force-unlock has the same shape. It removes a lock. It does not stop the process holding it. On the left, an apply was still running when its lock was forced open. A second apply then ran and wrote its state, the first one finished its migration anyway, and then failed to release a lock that was no longer its own. Before forcing a lock, confirm the owner it names has really stopped.

A Terraform setup has four parts that each have versions: the providers, the modules, the Terraform CLI and the backend. They move independently, so upgrade them independently, one at a time, with a plan as your evidence. For each upgrade, read the release notes for anything marked as breaking. Change exactly one version, in staging first. Then plan. For a pure upgrade, the plan you hope for is no changes, and anything else needs explaining before it goes further. This course has done two real upgrades. In chapter two, init dash upgrade moved the random provider from three point eight point one to three point nine point one, and the lock file diff showed it. And for this chapter, state applied with a release candidate of Terraform one point seventeen was read back by one point sixteen point six without complaint, because Terraform one point x keeps its state format compatible. Providers are different. A newer provider can upgrade the data it stores for a resource, and an older provider may then refuse to read it, so treat provider upgrades as one-way. Release candidates belong in test environments. And upgrade regularly: many small steps are far easier than one large jump.

Systems that grow usually stop fitting in one region or one account, and some span more than one cloud. Each of those is a different kind of boundary, and Terraform treats them differently. Regions are the mildest. One team can manage resources in several regions from a single state, using provider aliases from chapter two, or the per-resource region argument that newer AWS providers accept. Accounts are a security boundary, so they deserve separate state and separate roles, exactly as chapter eight described. The staging and production accounts each have their own, and shared services such as DNS or the state buckets themselves get an account and a state of their own too. Clouds are the strongest boundary. Each cloud is a different provider, with different resource types and different schemas, so there is no such thing as a resource definition that simply moves between them. What can cross is published values, such as a network address range or a DNS name. Portability is therefore a design choice, made at the level of module interfaces: a module can offer the same inputs and outputs everywhere, while its implementation stays specific to each provider.

Chapter four introduced splitting state to limit blast radius. Here is the trade-off in numbers. The same nine hundred instances were planned two ways: as one state, and as three states of three hundred. A destroy plan against the single state covers all nine hundred. Against the application's state, it covers three hundred and nothing else. Every plan of the large state refreshes everything and holds one lock for all of it. Even with terraform data, which needs no network at all, the large plan took four times as long; with real providers, every instance is an API call, and the gap grows. What one state gives you in return is simplicity. References between parts are direct, and Terraform orders everything for you. Split the state, and plans get faster, locks and permissions get separate, but ordering across states becomes your problem: something must apply the network before the application, and pass values between them through published outputs. So split deliberately, along ownership and rate of change, as chapter four suggested, and when objects need to move between states, use chapter six's removed and import blocks rather than editing state by hand.

That is the whole lifecycle. It started with one small resource and a single idea: configuration describes what should exist, Terraform compares it with what it has recorded, and a plan shows the difference before anything changes. Every chapter since has built on that. How configuration expresses intent, and how dependencies and identity shape a plan. Why state matters, and how to protect it. How modules package configuration, and how to adopt and refactor without destroying what you meant to keep. What evidence each kind of check provides. How credentials and secrets leak, and how teams review, apply and govern changes. And finally, how to diagnose and recover when something goes wrong. You should now be able to explain how a plan is derived and what it cannot show, who owns each object and where that ownership is recorded, and what evidence supports a change. To go further, rebuild these examples yourself and break them on purpose. Read the documentation for the provider and backend versions you actually run. Review real plans with someone experienced. And remember that understanding is the start. Responsibility for production comes with demonstrated deployments and demonstrated recoveries.
